title: Lower Academic Standards Can Perpetuate Unfairness
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that well-intentioned moves to lower academic standards, from dropping the SAT at the University of California to abolishing New York's Regents exams, end up harming the disadvantaged students they aim to protect. She contrasts Berkeley professor Zvezdelina Stankova's warnings about students years behind in math with defenses of the status quo from Miriam Pawel and Regents board member Felicia Thomas-Williams. Wexler rejects explanations that blame Covid or outdated test passages, pointing to cognitive science showing that comprehension depends on background knowledge rather than transferable skills. She uses Nikole Hannah-Jones's account of her daughter's math gaps, including a principal's admission about racism under the guise of antiracism, to show how the quest for fairness can backfire. The piece then lays out what works: orderly school environments, explicit instruction, a content-rich sequenced curriculum, and teacher support grounded in cognitive science, with England's PISA results offered as suggestive evidence. Her conclusion is that lowering standards only kicks the can down the road.
points: Wexler contends that the fish-can't-climb-trees argument quietly assumes some children are naturally incapable of mastering complex academic subjects.
She argues that inference and comprehension depend heavily on background knowledge, so skills practiced on familiar topics will not transfer to complex texts on unfamiliar ones.
Her prescription combines calm school-wide behavior systems, explicit instruction including in writing, content-rich sequenced curriculum, and ongoing cognitively informed teacher support.
England's rise in PISA rankings and a narrower-than-average socioeconomic gap are cited as suggestive evidence for a knowledge-rich approach.
For underprepared college students, she suggests community college remediation followed by transfer rather than lowering selective universities' standards.
quotes: It's true that people with college degrees, especially from a school like Berkeley, are likely to go farther in life than people without them.
